title: Your own verse
hookLine: the tradition of an awakening verse: a line spoken from what you've seen

lines: THE BOOK IS NAMED FOR IT.
cards: Then, knowing the meaning of this, on that occasion, he spoke this inspired verse. That sentence, give or take, closes story after story in a small book of the Pali canon.
Something happens: monks debate which of two kings is richer, boys beat a snake with a stick, a monk sits through pain without complaint. The Buddha sees it.
And a verse comes out of him, not prepared, not polished, spoken because of what he just saw. The book is named after that kind of verse.

teach.h: A VERSE THAT RISES FROM SEEING.
teach.b: First, the word. Udana is an inspired utterance: a verse that rises out of a moment of seeing. The Udana, the book, collects them, each with its story first and its verse after.
Bhaddiya, sighing ah, what bliss under his tree, is one of its stories. Second, the first one. The book opens just after the awakening.
The Buddha sits under the tree, and in the first part of the night he attends to how things arise from causes.

Then he speaks: when things become clear to someone ardent and absorbed, his doubts all vanish, because he understands each thing along with its cause. It isn't a hymn. It's a report of what he's just seen.

teach.h: THE ELDERS SPOKE THE SAME WAY.
teach.b: Their songs are not all called udanas, but tradition says the elders spoke theirs the same way, on the day something came clear: Subhuti's hut, Rahula's double fortune, Nanda's plain confession.
A verse spoken from seeing, not from wishing. That's what links the book and the songs. Fourth, what it isn't.

teach.h: NOT A PRAYER, NOT A VOW.
teach.b: An udana isn't a prayer, and it isn't a vow. It doesn't ask for anything or promise anything. It says: this is so.
And the verses in this book are brief. That leaves room for anyone who sits, at any stage, to find a line rising out of something they've actually seen.
Not a verse about awakening. A verse about the rain on the roof, or the moment the anger went quiet.

how: The Udana is part of the Khuddaka Nikaya in the Pali canon; Theravada teachers draw on its stories and verses, and its opening verse is linked with the night of the awakening.

o: a verse inspired by a moment of seeing
a prayer asking for help on the path
a vow made at the start of a retreat

p: doubts vanish when causes are seen
a story first, a verse after

s: an udana is a carefully drafted poem
it's a verse spoken on the occasion, out of what was just seen.
the Udana opens just after the awakening
the Buddha sits under the tree attending to how things arise from causes, and then he speaks.
an udana is a kind of prayer asking for help
it asks for nothing and promises nothing. it says: this is so.

games.q: in a story from the Udana, the Buddha has just watched something happen and understood it. what comes next?
o: he writes a long explanation for the monks.
he keeps the insight to himself.
a short verse comes out of him, on that occasion.
games.why: the book's refrain: knowing the meaning of this, on that occasion, he spoke this inspired verse.

practice: Look back over these days of sitting for a moment when something shifted, even a little: a breath that went long on its own, a thought that let go, a sound that was just a sound.
Let one moment come, and let one plain sentence come out of it, from what you noticed rather than what you hope for: this is so.

wordCard.voice: Udana. An inspired utterance: a short verse spoken out of a moment of seeing, not prepared and not polished. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali udana: an inspired utterance, and the name of the book that collects them.

carryVoice: Your line: this is so. A verse can be as plain as what you saw. Day eight hundred fourteen, done.
